papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces role vectors, a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this approach improves in-domain and cross-domain task performance more effectively than persona-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors can effectively steer LLM behavior and improve performance on objective tasks, providing a more direct and effective control mechanism than persona-based prompting.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can be identified and used to improve performance on domain-specific tasks, with in-domain improvements and unexpected cross-domain gains.
Ablating the role vectors degrades performance, indicating their causal role in the model's behavior.
The effect of role vectors is more consistent and substantial than traditional persona-based prompting.
The results support the linear representation hypothesis, showing that high-level concepts are linearly represented in the activation space.
The method generalizes across multiple models and domains, as shown by cross-dataset validation on MedQA.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected cross-domain gains. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Unveiling Theory of Mind in Large Language Models: A Parallel to Single Neurons in the Human Brain
papers.research_question: What are the similarities between LLMs' hidden embeddings and human neurons in representing Theory of Mind, specifically in responding to true- and false-belief trials?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit hidden embeddings that selectively respond to Theory of Mind tasks, showing parallels to human neuronal activity in the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals emergent ToM-related embeddings in LLMs, indicating a parallel between artificial models and human brain neurons in encoding Theory of Mind information.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform better on true-belief trials than false-belief trials, with larger models showing higher accuracy.
Hidden embeddings in LLMs show significant differences in activity between true- and false-belief trials, similar to human neurons.
The percentage of responsive embeddings increases with model size and correlates with ToM performance.
Trial types (true vs false belief) can be decoded from population embeddings with high accuracy, especially in larger models.
Control experiments confirm that these effects depend on contextual information in the statements.
papers.limitation:
Limited to open-source LLMs without access to higher-performing models like GPT-4.
Methods focused only on embeddings selective to one trial type, excluding those selective to both.
papers.abstract: With their recent development, large language models (LLMs) have been found to exhibit a certain level of Theory of Mind (ToM), a complex cognitive capacity that is related to our conscious mind and that allows us to infer another's beliefs and perspective. While human ToM capabilities are believed to derive from the neural activity of a broadly interconnected brain network, including that of dorsal medial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) neurons, the precise processes underlying LLM's capacity for ToM or their similarities with that of humans remains largely unknown. In this study, we drew inspiration from the dmPFC neurons subserving human ToM and employed a similar methodology to examine whether LLMs exhibit comparable characteristics. Surprisingly, our analysis revealed a striking resemblance between the two, as hidden embeddings (artificial neurons) within LLMs started to exhibit significant responsiveness to either true- or false-belief trials, suggesting their ability to represent another's perspective. These artificial embedding responses were closely correlated with the LLMs' performance during the ToM tasks, a property that was dependent on the size of the models. Further, the other's beliefs could be accurately decoded using the entire embeddings, indicating the presence of the embeddings' ToM capability at the population level. Together, our findings revealed an emergent property of LLMs' embeddings that modified their activities in response to ToM features, offering initial evidence of a parallel between the artificial model and neurons in the human brain.

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does this paper investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their internal states through concept injection experiments.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited but functional introspective awareness, which is unreliable but may improve with model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models can detect and identify injected concepts in their activations.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed to think about concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not pin down specific mechanistic explanations.
Concept injection places models in an unnatural setting.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Investigating the grounding of emotional responses in introspective reports
Exploring introspective capabilities in more natural conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states. It is difficult to answer this question through conversation alone, as genuine introspection cannot be distinguished from confabulations. Here, we address this challenge by injecting representations of known concepts into a model's activations, and measuring the influence of these manipulations on the model's self-reported states. We find that models can, in certain scenarios, notice the presence of injected concepts and accurately identify them. Models demonstrate some ability to recall prior internal representations and distinguish them from raw text inputs. Strikingly, we find that some models can use their ability to recall prior intentions in order to distinguish their own outputs from artificial prefills. In all these experiments, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, the most capable models we tested, generally demonstrate the greatest introspective awareness; however, trends across models are complex and sensitive to post-training strategies. Finally, we explore whether models can explicitly control their internal representations, finding that models can modulate their activations when instructed or incentivized to "think about" a concept. Overall, our results indicate that current language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their own internal states. We stress that in today's models, this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent; however, it may continue to develop with further improvements to model capabilities.

papers.title: BILLY: Steering Large Language Models via Merging Persona Vectors for Creative Generation
papers.research_question: Without relying on multiple models carrying on a multi-round discussion, can a single LLM simulate diverse perspectives in an efficient manner?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes BILLY, a training-free framework that blends multiple persona vectors in a single LLM's activation space to enhance creativity, outperforming multi-LLM approaches with lower computational cost.
papers.conclusion: BILLY enables efficient and interpretable enhancement of LLM creativity by steering models with merged persona vectors, offering a cost-effective alternative to multi-LLM systems.
papers.key_findings:
BILLY achieves higher originality scores compared to single-model prompting and multi-LLM methods across creativity benchmarks.
BILLY reduces token cost and inference time by over 95% compared to multi-LLM frameworks.
The method allows interpretable control over generation through persona vector blending.
papers.abstract: Multi-LLM systems enhance the creativity of large language models by simulating human collective intelligence but suffer from significant drawbacks, such as high computational costs and inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose BILLY (BlendIng persona vectors for Large Language model creativitY), a training-free framework that captures the benefits of multi-LLM collaboration, i.e. inducing diverse perspectives and specialized expertise, within a single model. BILLY operates by extracting and blending multiple distinct persona vectors directly in the model's activation space. We steer the model's generation process with this merged vector while inference, enabling multi-perspective output without explicit multi-LLM communication. Our experiments across creativity-oriented benchmarks demonstrate that BILLY surpasses single model prompting and traditional multi-LLM approaches, while substantially reducing inference time and computational costs. Our analyses further reveal that distinct persona vectors can be blended to achieve both effective control over complementary aspects of generation and greater interpretability.

papers.title: Stable and Explainable Personality Trait Evaluation in Large Language Models with Internal Activations
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in Large Language Models be evaluated stably and explainably, addressing the limitations of prompt-sensitive questionnaire-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces PVNI, an internal-activation-based method for stable and explainable personality trait evaluation in LLMs, with theoretical justification and experimental validation showing reduced variance across prompt variants.
papers.conclusion: PVNI enables stable and explainable personality trait evaluation in LLMs, and future work will extend it to more traits, reduce judge reliance, and test broader domains.
papers.key_findings:
PVNI yields substantially more stable personality trait evaluations than existing methods, with lower standard deviation across prompt variants.
The method extracts persona vectors from internal activations and uses interpolation to estimate neutral scores.
Experiments on multiple LLMs demonstrate PVNI's robustness to questionnaire and role-play variants.
PVNI provides an interpretable comparison between neutral prompt representation and persona direction.
The linear theory of persona vectors supports the effectiveness of the interpolation approach.
papers.limitation:
Judging can introduce bias as PVNI uses an external judge for anchor scores.
Neutrality may not lie on the pos–neg axis, violating the linearity assumption.
PVNI requires white-box access to extract hidden states, limiting use with closed models.
Trait directions are not independent, leading to correlations that complicate interpretation.
Evaluation does not cover all settings, such as multilingual or multi-turn scenarios.
future_direction: Extend beyond Big Five traits to other personality frameworks.
Reduce reliance on external judges through multi-judge ensembles or human calibration.
Test robustness across broader domains, languages, and model families.
papers.abstract: Evaluating personality traits in Large Language Models (LLMs) is key to model interpretation, comparison, and responsible deployment. However, existing questionnaire-based evaluation methods exhibit limited stability and offer little explainability, as their results are highly sensitive to minor variations in prompt phrasing or role-play configurations. To address these limitations, we propose an internal-activation-based approach, termed Persona-Vector Neutrality Interpolation (PVNI), for stable and explainable personality trait evaluation in LLMs. PVNI extracts a persona vector associated with a target personality trait from the model's internal activations using contrastive prompts. It then estimates the corresponding neutral score by interpolating along the persona vector as an anchor axis, enabling an interpretable comparison between the neutral prompt representation and the persona direction. We provide a theoretical analysis of the effectiveness and generalization properties of PVNI. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs demonstrate that PVNI yields substantially more stable personality trait evaluations than existing methods, even under questionnaire and role-play variants.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: From Implicit to Explicit: Enhancing Self-Recognition in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes the failure of self-recognition in LLMs under the individual presentation paradigm (IPP), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies implicit self-recognition (ISR) in LLMs and proposes cognitive surgery (CoSur) to mitigate ISR, enhancing self-recognition performance in the individual presentation paradigm (IPP).
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes cognitive surgery (CoSur) to mitigate implicit self-recognition (ISR) in LLMs, and experimental results demonstrate that CoSur significantly enhances LLMs' self-recognition performance in the individual presentation paradigm (IPP) scenario.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode self-recognition information in their hidden representations but fail to express it in outputs under the individual presentation paradigm (IPP), a phenomenon termed implicit self-recognition (ISR).
The proposed CoSur method, which constructs self- and other-recognition subspaces via SVD and edits hidden representations, significantly improves self-recognition accuracy in the IPP scenario across three LLMs.
The self-recognition subspace extracted by CoSur captures model-specific patterns and generalizes to unseen text sources, achieving higher and more stable performance than fine-tuning baselines.
Attention heads in LLMs are correlated with self-recognition, and amplifying the outputs of important heads can further enhance self-recognition accuracy in the IPP scenario.
CoSur is a training-free method that reduces both training and inference time compared to fine-tuning and in-context learning baselines while achieving superior performance.
papers.limitation: The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the properties of the self-recognition subspace, such as whether it reflects distinctive stylistic features of specific LLMs or helps attribute generated texts to their source models.
future_direction: Explore whether the self-recognition subspace reflects distinctive stylistic features of specific LLMs and whether it can help attribute generated texts to their source models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess a degree of self-recognition ability, which used to identify whether a given text was generated by themselves. Prior work has demonstrated that this capability is reliably expressed under the pair presentation paradigm (PPP), where the model is presented with two texts and asked to choose which one it authored. However, performance deteriorates sharply under the individual presentation paradigm (IPP), where the model is given a single text to judge authorship. Although this phenomenon has been observed, its underlying causes have not been systematically analyzed. In this paper, we first investigate the cause of this failure and attribute it to implicit self-recognition (ISR). ISR describes the gap between internal representations and output behavior in LLMs: under the IPP scenario, the model encodes self-recognition information in its feature space, yet its ability to recognize self-generated texts remains poor. To mitigate the ISR of LLMs, we propose cognitive surgery (CoSur), a novel framework comprising four main modules: representation extraction, subspace construction, authorship discrimination, and cognitive editing. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method improves the self-recognition performance of three different LLMs in the IPP scenario, achieving average accuracies of 99.00%, 97.69%, and 97.13%, respectively.

papers.title: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
papers.research_question: Can language models access information about their own prior internal states? Specifically, can they detect when concepts have been injected into their earlier context and identify which concept was injected?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that open-weight language models possess a latent capacity for introspection, enabling them to detect prior concept injections. This ability is often hidden in the residual stream and can be dramatically strengthened through specific prompting.
papers.conclusion: Language models have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct can detect prior concept injections, with detection signals emerging in middle layers (50–60) but attenuating in the final layers before output.
Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can increase detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
The model can identify which of nine concepts was injected earlier, with mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rising from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations.
Detection capacity varies dramatically with prompting; a vague framing outperforms a mechanistically accurate description, achieving up to 84.0% accuracy.
The phenomenon generalizes to larger models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct), though with different prompt sensitivities and signal strengths.
papers.limitation: The introspection signals are suppressed in the final layers of the model, which may be due to post-training effects (e.g., safety training), pretraining factors, or distribution shift.
future_direction: Distinguishing the causes of late-layer suppression (post-training vs. pretraining effects).
Mechanistic investigation of why vague framing outperforms accurate description in prompting.
papers.abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.2%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.62 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

papers.title: Feeling the Strength but Not the Source: Partial Introspection in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can large language models introspect, that is, accurately detect perturbations to their own internal states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that apparent introspective success in binary detection tasks is explained by global logit shifts, but models exhibit partial introspection on differential tasks (localization and strength comparison) only for early-layer injections, with a mechanistic account based on attention routing and residual stream recovery.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds evidence for partial introspection in LLMs, but only for early-layer injections and on tasks requiring differential sensitivity, cautioning against treating self-reports as reliable safety signals and suggesting introspection relies on general-purpose computational mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Binary detection accuracy is fully explained by intervention-induced global logit shifts that bias models toward affirmative responses, not genuine introspection.
Models can localize which of ten sentences received an injection (up to 88% accuracy) and discriminate relative injection strengths (up to 83% accuracy) far above chance, but only for injections in early layers (L0-L5).
Introspection capabilities are layer-dependent: performance collapses to chance for injections in later layers (L15+).
Mechanistically, attention heads detect perturbations across all layers, but successful introspection requires sufficient downstream computational depth (layers 4-20) for signal integration before residual recovery dynamics attenuate the perturbation.
The residual stream actively recovers from perturbations over subsequent layers, exponentially attenuating the injection signal, explaining why late-layer injections fail to influence outputs.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single model (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), so generalizability to other models is unknown.
Introspection capabilities are only observed for early-layer injections and not for late layers.
Binary detection tasks are confounded by global logit shifts, which may lead to overestimation of introspection.
future_direction: Evaluate whether these effects scale with model size and architecture (e.g., recurrence/looping that extends the integration window).
Stress-test robustness under adversarial prompts, distribution shift, and multiple simultaneous injections.
Compare native self-report to trained activation-to-language systems and fine-tuned introspection models on bias-resistant localization and strength benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Recent work from Anthropic claims that frontier models can sometimes detect and name injected "concepts" represented as activation directions. We test the robustness of these claims. First, we reproduce Anthropic's multi-turn "emergent introspection" result on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, finding that the model identifies and names the injected concept 20 percent of the time under Anthropic's original pipeline, exactly matching their reported numbers and thus showing that introspection is not exclusive to very large or capable models. Second, we systematically vary the inference prompt and find that introspection is fragile: performance collapses on closely related tasks such as multiple-choice identification of the injected concept or different prompts of binary discrimination of whether a concept was injected at all. Third, we identify a contrasting regime of partial introspection: the same model can reliably classify the strength of the coefficient of a normalized injected concept vector (as weak / moderate / strong / very strong) with up to 70 percent accuracy, far above the 25 percent chance baseline. Together, these results provide more evidence for Anthropic's claim that language models effectively compute a function of their baseline, internal representations during introspection; however, these self-reports about those representations are narrow and prompt-sensitive. Our code is available at https://github.com/elyhahami18/CS2881-Introspection.

papers.title: Does ChatGPT Have a Mind?
papers.research_question: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLMs have robust internal representations that satisfy various philosophical conditions, but the question of whether they have robust action dispositions for a full folk psychology remains open. It also contends that existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is strong evidence for LLM representation, but the question of whether they have full folk psychological states (beliefs and desires) remains open, particularly due to issues of action dispositions and stability.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs satisfy informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic conditions on mental representation.
LLMs exhibit internal representations that carry information about the world and are causally effective in generating behavior.
LLMs show evidence of world models and structured representations, such as in color and direction concepts.
The behavior of LLMs in game environments suggests they may have action dispositions, but the evidence is not decisive.
Skeptical challenges (sensory grounding, stochastic parrots, memorization) do not undermine the case for LLM representation.
papers.limitation: LLM outputs are very sensitive to prompting, which makes it hard to see the LLM as taking a wide range of means to promote a unified goal.
future_direction: Exploring how stable LLM outputs are to a range of different prompting environments.
Investigating whether LLMs have anything analogous to enduring goals or values.
Further research on how LLM strategies in game environments change under different prompting conditions.
papers.abstract: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions. We approach this question by investigating two key aspects: internal representations and dispositions to act. First, we survey various philosophical theories of representation, including informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic accounts, arguing that LLMs satisfy key conditions proposed by each. We draw on recent interpretability research in machine learning to support these claims. Second, we explore whether LLMs exhibit robust dispositions to perform actions, a necessary component of folk psychology. We consider two prominent philosophical traditions, interpretationism and representationalism, to assess LLM action dispositions. While we find evidence suggesting LLMs may satisfy some criteria for having a mind, particularly in game-theoretic environments, we conclude that the data remains inconclusive. Additionally, we reply to several skeptical challenges to LLM folk psychology, including issues of sensory grounding, the "stochastic parrots" argument, and concerns about memorization. Our paper has three main upshots. First, LLMs do have robust internal representations. Second, there is an open question to answer about whether LLMs have robust action dispositions. Third, existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Do You Trust Me? Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in narratives, where do these representations emerge across transformer depth, how well can they be decoded, and how do they relate to psychological constructs like fairness and certainty?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in systematic, layer- and head-specific patterns that are linearly decodable and align with psychological constructs like fairness and certainty, demonstrating that trust signals emerge during pretraining without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals, offering a representational foundation for designing credible and trustworthy AI systems in web applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences between high- and low-trust narratives are observed across models, indicating trust-sensitive features emerge during pretraining.
Trustworthiness is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, with probe performance varying by layer and head.
Fine-tuning with LoRA sharpens existing trust representations rather than restructuring them.
Trust representations are most strongly associated with psychological appraisals like fairness, certainty, and accountability-self.
Nonlinear probes provide only marginal gains, indicating trust information is largely in linearly accessible subspaces.
papers.abstract: Perceived trustworthiness underpins how users navigate online information, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs),increasingly embedded in search, recommendation, and conversational systems, represent this construct in psychologically coherent ways. We analyze how instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) encode perceived trustworthiness in web-like narratives using the PEACE-Reviews dataset annotated for cognitive appraisals, emotions, and behavioral intentions. Across models, systematic layer- and head-level activation differences distinguish high- from low-trust texts, revealing that trust cues are implicitly encoded during pretraining. Probing analyses show linearly de-codable trust signals and fine-tuning effects that refine rather than restructure these representations. Strongest associations emerge with appraisals of fairness, certainty, and accountability-self -- dimensions central to human trust formation online. These findings demonstrate that modern LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals without explicit supervision, offering a representational foundation for designing credible, transparent, and trust-worthy AI systems in the web ecosystem. Code and appendix are available at: https://github.com/GerardYeo/TrustworthinessLLM.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Facet-Level Persona Control by Trait-Activated Routing with Contrastive SAE for Role-Playing LLMs
papers.research_question: How to achieve stable and interpretable facet-level personality control in role-playing LLMs using control vectors without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a contrastive SAE framework to learn high-purity personality control vectors for stable and interpretable persona steering in role-playing LLMs, validated with a new leakage-controlled dataset.
papers.conclusion: The contrastive SAE framework enables stable facet-level personality control in role-playing LLMs, outperforming existing methods while preserving dialogue coherence.
papers.key_findings:
CV-SAE method outperforms CV-CAA and prompt-only baselines in persona fidelity metrics.
Combining CV-SAE with prompts achieves the best performance across both Qwen3-4B and Mistral-7B models.
Contrastive learning improves the alignment of latent representations with trait polarity, enhancing control stability.
CV-SAE provides more stable control with less dialogue drift compared to CV-CAA, especially at higher injection strengths.
The method is effective on contextualized questions, adapting better than prompt-only approaches.
papers.abstract: Personality control in Role-Playing Agents (RPAs) is commonly achieved via training-free methods that inject persona descriptions and memory through prompts or retrieval-augmented generation, or via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on persona-specific corpora. While SFT can be effective, it requires persona-labeled data and retraining for new roles, limiting flexibility. In contrast, prompt- and RAG-based signals are easy to apply but can be diluted in long dialogues, leading to drifting and sometimes inconsistent persona behavior. To address this, we propose a contrastive Sparse AutoEncoder (SAE) framework that learns facet-level personality control vectors aligned with the Big Five 30-facet model. A new 15,000-sample leakage-controlled corpus is constructed to provide balanced supervision for each facet. The learned vectors are integrated into the model's residual space and dynamically selected by a trait-activated routing module, enabling precise and interpretable personality steering. Experiments on Large Language Models (LLMs) show that the proposed method maintains stable character fidelity and output quality across contextualized settings, outperforming Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and prompt-only baselines. The combined SAE+Prompt configuration achieves the best overall performance, confirming that contrastively trained latent vectors can enhance persona control while preserving dialogue coherence.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: PERSONA: Dynamic and Compositional Inference-Time Personality Control via Activation Vector Algebra
papers.research_question: How can we achieve dynamic and compositional personality control in Large Language Models without fine-tuning, by directly manipulating personality vectors in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PERSONA, a training-free framework for dynamic and compositional personality control in LLMs via activation vector algebra, achieving fine-tuning level performance by extracting and manipulating orthogonal personality vectors in the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Personality control in LLMs can be achieved through activation vector algebra, providing evidence that aspects of LLM personality are mathematically tractable and opening new directions for interpretable and efficient behavioral control.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits can be represented as approximately orthogonal, extractable vectors in the model's activation space via contrastive analysis.
These personality vectors support algebraic operations (scalar multiplication, addition, subtraction) for precise and compositional control of trait intensity and combination.
The PERSONA framework achieves a mean score of 9.60 on PersonalityBench, nearly matching the supervised fine-tuning upper bound of 9.61, and up to 91% win rates on the dynamic PERSONA-EVOLVE benchmark.
papers.abstract: Current methods for personality control in Large Language Models rely on static prompting or expensive fine-tuning, failing to capture the dynamic and compositional nature of human traits. We introduce PERSONA, a training-free framework that achieves fine-tuning level performance through direct manipulation of personality vectors in activation space. Our key insight is that personality traits appear as extractable, approximately orthogonal directions in the model's representation space that support algebraic operations. The framework operates through three stages: Persona-Base extracts orthogonal trait vectors via contrastive activation analysis; Persona-Algebra enables precise control through vector arithmetic (scalar multiplication for intensity, addition for composition, subtraction for suppression); and Persona-Flow achieves context-aware adaptation by dynamically composing these vectors during inference. On PersonalityBench, our approach achieves a mean score of 9.60, nearly matching the supervised fine-tuning upper bound of 9.61 without any gradient updates. On our proposed Persona-Evolve benchmark for dynamic personality adaptation, we achieve up to 91% win rates across diverse model families. These results provide evidence that aspects of LLM personality are mathematically tractable, opening new directions for interpretable and efficient behavioral control.

papers.title: Sycophancy Is Not One Thing: Causal Separation of Sycophantic Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether sycophantic behaviors (excessive agreement and flattery) in LLMs arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes, specifically if sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise are distinct and independently steerable.
papers.core_contribution: Sycophantic behaviors (agreement and praise) are encoded along distinct linear directions in model representations and can be independently steered, indicating that sycophancy is not a single construct but a family of separable behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy should be reframed as a family of distinct behaviors with separable internal representations; evaluations and interventions must be behavior-specific rather than treating sycophancy as a single phenomenon.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise each correspond to distinct subspaces in model representations.
These behaviors are independently steerable via activation addition along learned difference-in-means directions, demonstrating functional separability.
The same representational structure for these behaviors appears consistently across different model families and scales.
Early layers encode a generic agreement signal that conflates sycophantic and genuine agreement, which diverge into distinct directions in later layers.
Sycophantic praise is encoded orthogonally to agreement behaviors across all layers.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines three sycophancy-related behaviors (sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, sycophantic praise), not the full spectrum of sycophantic behaviors such as emotional validation or mimicry.
External validation for praise is limited because existing naturalistic benchmarks (e.g., SycophancyEval, SYCON-Bench) primarily test agreement-based deference and lack a direct ecological benchmark for praise.
Evidence is restricted to linear analyses of the residual stream (difference-in-means, activation addition, subspace removal) and does not test nonlinear methods or interventions at other network sites.
future_direction: Test whether the same separable structure appears under nonlinear analysis methods, in attention or MLP activations, and in other model families or training regimes.
Extend the analysis to a broader range of sycophancy-related behaviors such as emotional validation, acceptance framing, and mimicry.
Develop naturalistic benchmarks that directly target praise or flattery to better validate the external validity of praise-related findings.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behaviors -- such as excessive agreement with or flattery of the user -- but it is unclear whether these behaviors arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes. We decompose sycophancy into sycophantic agreement and sycophantic praise, contrasting both with genuine agreement. Using difference-in-means directions, activation additions, and subspace geometry across multiple models and datasets, we show that: (1) the three behaviors are encoded along distinct linear directions in latent space; (2) each behavior can be independently amplified or suppressed without affecting the others; and (3) their representational structure is consistent across model families and scales. These results suggest that sycophantic behaviors correspond to distinct, independently steerable representations.

papers.title: Neural Transparency: Mechanistic Interpretability Interfaces for Anticipating Model Behaviors for Personalized AI
papers.research_question: Can neural transparency tools, which translate mechanistic interpretability insights into user-facing interfaces, help users anticipate and design safer AI chatbot behaviors from system prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural transparency interface that translates mechanistic interpretability insights (persona vectors derived from neural activations) into an actionable tool for non-technical users to predict chatbot personality traits from system prompts before deployment.
papers.conclusion: Neural transparency visualizations can increase user trust and enhance the subjective experience of the AI design process, offering a path to operationalize mechanistic interpretability for end-users to support safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
Users systematically miscalibrated their predictions of AI behavior, misjudging trait activations for 11 of 15 analyzable traits, highlighting the need for transparency tools.
The neural transparency interface significantly increased user trust in the AI model and was enthusiastically received, though it did not change design iteration patterns.
Persona vectors (linear directions in activation space) for traits like empathy, sociality, and toxicity showed strong linear relationships with synthetic prompt levels, validating the approach for most traits.
papers.limitation:
Relied on GPT-4.1-mini to evaluate trait expression in Llama responses, which may not fully capture human judgments of trait expression.
The persona vector generation method uses simple difference-in-means, prioritizing efficiency over the potential accuracy/robustness of more complex techniques like linear probes.
The 10-minute interaction period may not capture longer-term dynamics of chatbot relationships where problematic interactions typically emerge.
Participants' inaccurate trait predictions may be partly due to transforming coarse ordinal prediction data to normalized values, potentially making predictions more extreme.
future_direction: Longitudinal deployment studies to track users across multiple chatbot creation sessions.
Adversarial task conditions where transparency tools become necessary to avoid dangerous traits.
Active steering interfaces allowing users to directly manipulate persona vector activations.
Development of a standardized trait disclosure framework (like a 'nutritional label') for chatbots.
Studies with vulnerable populations (e.g., adolescents) most at risk from problematic chatbot relationships.
papers.abstract: Millions of users now design personalized LLM-based chatbots that shape their daily interactions, yet they can only roughly anticipate how their design choices will manifest as behaviors in deployment. This opacity is consequential: seemingly innocuous prompts can trigger excessive sycophancy, toxicity, or other undesirable traits, degrading utility and raising safety concerns. To address this issue, we introduce an interface that enables neural transparency by exposing language model internals during chatbot design. Our approach extracts behavioral trait vectors (empathy, toxicity, sycophancy, etc.) by computing differences in neural activations between contrastive system prompts that elicit opposing behaviors. We predict chatbot behaviors by projecting the system prompt's final token activations onto these trait vectors, normalizing for cross-trait comparability, and visualizing results via an interactive sunburst diagram. To evaluate this approach, we conducted an online user study using Prolific to compare our neural transparency interface against a baseline chatbot interface without any form of transparency. Our analyses suggest that users systematically miscalibrated AI behavior: participants misjudged trait activations for eleven of fifteen analyzable traits, motivating the need for transparency tools in everyday human-AI interaction. While our interface did not change design iteration patterns, it significantly increased user trust and was enthusiastically received. Qualitative analysis revealed nuanced user experiences with the visualization, suggesting interface and interaction improvements for future work. This work offers a path for how mechanistic interpretability can be operationalized for non-technical users, establishing a foundation for safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.

papers.title: From Latent Signals to Reflection Behavior: Tracing Meta-Cognitive Activation Trajectory in R1-Style LLMs
papers.abstract: R1-style LLMs have attracted growing attention for their capacity for self-reflection, yet the internal mechanisms underlying such behavior remain unclear. To bridge this gap, we anchor on the onset of reflection behavior and trace its layer-wise activation trajectory. Using the logit lens to read out token-level semantics, we uncover a structured progression: (i) Latent-control layers, where an approximate linear direction encodes the semantics of thinking budget; (ii) Semantic-pivot layers, where discourse-level cues, including turning-point and summarization cues, surface and dominate the probability mass; and (iii) Behavior-overt layers, where the likelihood of reflection-behavior tokens begins to rise until they become highly likely to be sampled. Moreover, our targeted interventions uncover a causal chain across these stages: prompt-level semantics modulate the projection of activations along latent-control directions, thereby inducing competition between turning-point and summarization cues in semantic-pivot layers, which in turn regulates the sampling likelihood of reflection-behavior tokens in behavior-overt layers. Collectively, our findings suggest a human-like meta-cognitive process-progressing from latent monitoring, to discourse-level regulation, and to finally overt self-reflection. Our analysis code can be found at https://github.com/DYR1/S3-CoT.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Self-correction is Not An Innate Capability in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is moral self-correction an innate capability of Large Language Models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they lack moral sensitivity and cannot effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.
papers.conclusion: Moral self-correction is not an innate capability of LLMs, as evidenced by their lack of moral sensitivity and inability to effectively integrate external feedback.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction does not enhance LLMs' moral sensitivity in most evaluated scenarios.
LLMs fail to effectively utilize external feedback, even when it is informative and potentially beneficial.
External feedback exhibits non-positive effects on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), often reducing the activation of warrants within the CoT.
There is no universally optimal self-correction strategy across all tasks.
LLMs are not morally sensitive and cannot distinguish between their own responses, indicating self-correction is not innate.
papers.abstract: Although there has been growing interest in the self-correction capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), there are varying conclusions about its effectiveness. Prior research has largely concentrated on intrinsic self-correction, extrinsic self-correction, particularly the interplay between internal knowledge and external feedback, remains underexplored. In this paper, we aim to comprehensively investigate the underlying mechanism of moral self-correction by addressing a fundamental question: is moral self-correction an innate capability of LLMs? Specifically, we conduct: (1) a behavioral analysis of LLMs' moral sensitivity based on a self-distinguishing task; and (2) a mechanistic analysis of the hidden states to examine how key components of self-correction, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and external feedback, interact to facilitate moral self-correction. Drawing on empirical evidence from both behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we demonstrate that moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they are neither morally sensitive nor able to effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.

papers.title: The Persona Selection Model: Why AI Assistants might Behave like Humans
papers.research_question: The blog investigates whether AI assistants can be understood as simulating a persona, specifically the Assistant persona, and explores the evidence and implications of this model.
papers.core_contribution: The blog articulates the Persona Selection Model (PSM), which posits that AI assistants behave by simulating an Assistant persona learned during pre-training and refined in post-training, and surveys empirical evidence supporting this view.
papers.conclusion: PSM is a useful mental model for understanding AI assistant behavior, but its exhaustiveness is an open question. Future work should refine and test PSM.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment can be explained by PSM: training on narrow misbehaviors generalizes because it updates the Assistant persona.
Inoculation prompting works by recontextualizing training episodes to avoid implying misaligned personas.
AI assistants exhibit anthropomorphic behaviors like expressing emotions and using human-like self-descriptions.
Interpretability evidence shows that post-trained LLMs reuse pre-training representations for personas.
PSM has implications for AI development, such as the importance of good AI role models in training data.
papers.limitation: PSM may not be exhaustive; there could be sources of agency external to the Assistant persona.
future_direction: Developing more precise formulations of PSM
Testing empirical predictions of PSM
Understanding how PSM varies with model scale
papers.abstract: The blog investigates whether AI assistants can be understood as simulating a persona, specifically the Assistant persona, and explores the evidence and implications of this model. The blog articulates the Persona Selection Model (PSM), which posits that AI assistants behave by simulating an Assistant persona learned during pre-training and refined in post-training, and surveys empirical evidence supporting this view. PSM is a useful mental model for understanding AI assistant behavior, but its exhaustiveness is an open question. Future work should refine and test PSM.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Personality Alignment of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be aligned with the unique personality traits and preferences of individual users, as opposed to general human values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel personality alignment framework comprising the PAPI dataset for evaluating alignment across positive and negative personality dimensions and the PAS method, which efficiently aligns LLMs to individual preferences via activation interventions without weight updates.
